title: Competitor gap matrix — degradation handling and GTM hooks
body:
Purpose: quick reference for GTM / sales / product marketing to talk about how Redwood’s reliability and graceful degradation compare to competitors, with ready-to-use phrasing and short demo script ideas. Use this in deal prep, battlecards, and workshop slides.

Context: buyers care about two things in outages or partial capacity: (1) predictable user experience (what the end user sees) and (2) predictable economics and recovery (how the platform recovers and what costs/SLAs apply). Competitors typically trade off one for the other. This doc synthesizes gaps and gives succinct messaging and examples.

Audience: sales AE/SE, product marketing, solutions engineering, partner GTM.

How to use: reference the competitor matrix when preparing a pitch; pick 2–3 short proof points below; rehearse a 90s demo where you show fallback to a compatible model and transparent status updates.

Notes on tone: avoid technical jargon in customer-facing scripts; focus on predictability, transparency, and choice.
competitor_matrix: Cloud A (large cloud vendor): Degradation behavior: blunt endpoint throttling and retry; often returns 429s instead of structured fallbacks. Gap: limited customer-controlled fallbacks and poor observability. Redwood advantage: per-route fallback policies and token-level cost/latency tracing so customers see what was served and why.

API Provider B (LLM API specialist): Degradation behavior: auto-switch to smaller model without routing transparency; limited multi-region failover. Gap: opaque quality regressions and no customer opt-in controls. Redwood advantage: pinned versions + automatic variant rollouts with canary and rollback + explicit downgrade labeling in responses.

Self-hosted Runtime C (open-source infra): Degradation behavior: relies on operator-run scripts; recovery is manual and inconsistent. Gap: no turnkey SLA or enterprise-grade routing. Redwood advantage: SLA-backed Dedicated options and managed multi-region routing with policy-based fallbacks.

Vertical Player D (industry-specific vendor): Degradation behavior: serves cached canned answers for known prompts, otherwise blocks requests. Gap: inconsistent UX and brittle coverage outside known templates. Redwood advantage: prefix/KV caching plus graceful partial responses and structured function-like fallback outputs to preserve UX continuity.

Edge Provider E (latency-first): Degradation behavior: returns low-latency but truncated answers when under pressure; no quality monitoring. Gap: stealth regressions that break trust. Redwood advantage: quality monitoring tied to eval sets and automated regression alerts that notify customers and recommend rollback profiles.
key_messages: Predictable continuity not opacity: we prioritize transparent, documented fallback paths over silent failures.
Choice-preserving degradation: customers can opt for quality-first, latency-first, or cost-constrained fallback rules per route.
Observable economics: token-level cost breakdown and fallback-attribution so customers know unit economics during incidents.
SLA + managed fallback: Dedicated plans include predictable throughput and managed multi-region failover with clear SLOs.
Fast recovery + safe rollouts: canary rollouts, automatic rollback on quality regressions, and fallbacks that maintain app invariants.
incident_templates: Short CS script (customer-facing): "We detected elevated latency in Region X at 03:12 UTC. Your traffic was automatically routed to a compatible model variant in Region Y to maintain availability; responses may show a small change in phrasing for 8–12 minutes while caches warm. We’ll follow up with a detailed timeline and compensation if your SLA threshold was impacted."

Sales Q&A quickline: "If a region is degraded, we can route to an alternate region or a model variant with equivalent behavior; we provide pre-approved fallback policies you can inspect during onboarding. That avoids surprise quality regressions."

Executive status excerpt: "Impact: partial capacity in eu-west-1 affecting 3% of requests; mitigation: automatic multi-region reroute executed at 03:20 UTC; customer-visible change: minor tone variance due to variant mapping; next steps: postmortem and an opt-in conservative fallback policy for affected accounts."
demo_scripts: SE demo (90s): 1) Show baseline: call /v1/generate pinned to model v1.2. 2) Trigger simulated region failover in console. 3) Show same request auto-routed to v1.2-compatible quantized variant with explicit 'fallback' metadata in response. 4) Open Console > Tracing to show the fallback event and token cost delta. Talking points: predictable UX, visible change, cost transparency.

PM-led technical demo (3–5 min): 1) Show policy editor with per-route rules (latency threshold, quality threshold, allowed variants). 2) Flip policy to 'latency-first' and replay requests to show decreased p99 and small quality delta. 3) Run built-in eval suite to show automated regression alert. Talking points: customer control, measurable trade-offs.

GTM customer workshop (15 min): run a tabletop where attendees pick a fallback strategy for their app (e.g., search vs. creative chat) and we walk through expected UX and cost implications using Redwood’s model recommendations tool.
metrics_to_highlight: percentage of traffic served by cache/prefix-KV during incident
model-variant-change-rate (how often rollback or canary was triggered)
SLA impact window and any credit calculation examples
action_items: Create a short slide deck (4 slides) for AEs that shows: matrix + 90s demo steps + 2 customer scripts.
Add a sample API response payload example with a 'fallback_reason' field for use in SE demos and docs.
Coordinate with product to add a one-click demo toggle in the Console to simulate region failover for workshops.
Build one-page battlecard for top 3 competitors emphasizing observability and customer-controlled fallback policies.
Run a tabletop with 3 pilot accounts to validate messaging and adjust example compensation wording.
